--- title: "Tutorial 3 · Support vector machines" subtitle: "Session 4 · Day 1, 15.50–17.00 · Slides 04" --- ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## What you will do See what shape of boundary an SVM draws and why; fit a linear, a polynomial and a radial-kernel SVM on the honest predictor set through the same workflow; learn which pre-processing an SVM cannot live without; and compare kernels honestly on the five folds. **Time:** 25 min live coding + 15 min *Your turn*. ::: ## 0 · Start ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # WHERE WE ARE --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # T1 = the pipeline + logistic baseline (replayed by R/prep_nhms.R). T2 = trees and the random forest, fitted # with fit_resamples() on the same dm_folds and the same cls_metrics. NEW TODAY: the second family - support # vector machines - and the first model for which the recipe's normalisation step is not optional. source("R/prep_nhms.R") library(patchwork) library(future) plan(multisession, workers = max(1, parallel::detectCores() - 1)) ``` ::: ## 1 · The idea, in four pictures ::: {.callout-note} ## In one paragraph Start with one predictor and two classes. A **threshold** classifies, but a point just over it is called positive even when it looks like the negatives. The **maximal-margin classifier** puts the boundary halfway between the closest members of the two classes — as far from both as possible. One outlier drags that boundary into a terrible place, so we allow some points inside the margin or on the wrong side: a **soft margin**, whose generosity is set by cross-validation. That is a **support vector classifier**; the *support vectors* are the few points that touch or cross the margin — the only ones that matter. In two dimensions the boundary is a line, in three a plane, in *p* a hyperplane — still straight. When the classes overlap so that no straight boundary works, a **kernel** maps the data into a higher dimension where they *are* separable by a hyperplane, and the boundary projected back is curved. The kernel trick means you never compute the high-dimensional coordinates, only similarities between pairs of points. ::: ![](../images/gen/boundaries_toy.png){fig-align="center" width="85%"} Two kernels you will use: | Kernel | parsnip | Shape | Flexibility knob | |---|---|---|---| | Linear | `svm_linear(cost)` | hyperplane | — | | Polynomial | `svm_poly(cost, degree, scale_factor)` | polynomial curve | `degree`: 1 = linear, 2–3 = gentle curves, higher = wiggly | | Radial basis (RBF) | `svm_rbf(cost, rbf_sigma)` | Gaussian bumps around support vectors; can enclose islands | `rbf_sigma`: large = narrow bumps = wiggly; small = wide bumps = smooth | And the knob every kernel shares: **`cost`** — the penalty for a point violating the margin. High cost → narrow margin, fits the training data closely, overfits. Low cost → wide margin, underfits. Tune it on a log₂ scale. ## 2 · What an SVM needs from the recipe Two non-negotiables: 1. **Numeric predictors** — SVMs compute distances; "Indian" has no distance from "Malay". `step_dummy()`. 2. **Scaled predictors** — otherwise `hh_income` (thousands) defines the distance and `age` (tens) is ignored. `step_normalize()`. `dm_rec` already does both, which is why it was written that way in Tutorial 1. One engine-specific wrinkle: `kernlab::ksvm()` quietly standardises numeric inputs itself (`scaled = TRUE` is its default), so with this engine an unscaled recipe is *rescued* behind your back. Other SVM implementations (`LiblineaR`, `e1071` with `scale = FALSE`, anything you write in Python) do not, and neither do the neural networks this afternoon — keep the scaling in the recipe, where it is visible, versioned and applied identically at prediction time. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dm_rec ``` ::: ## 3 · Three kernels, one workflow ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svm_lin_spec <- svm_linear(cost = 1) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification") svm_poly_spec <- svm_poly(cost = 1, degree = 2) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification") svm_rbf_spec <- svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification") ``` ::: `rbf_sigma = 0.005` is a reasonable start for ~45 scaled predictors (kernlab's own heuristic, `sigest()`, lands nearby). Leave it out and kernlab estimates it for you. Fit the RBF version once and look at what came back: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} svm_rbf_fit <- workflow(dm_rec, svm_rbf_spec) |> fit(dm_train) svm_rbf_fit |> extract_fit_engine() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Support Vector Machine object of class "ksvm" SV type: C-svc (classification) parameter : cost C = 1 Gaussian Radial Basis kernel function. Hyperparameter : sigma = 0.005 Number of Support Vectors : 1086 Objective Function Value : -907.9629 Training error : 0.115779 Probability model included. ``` ::: ::: Note the **number of support vectors** — the people that define the boundary — and that kernlab fitted a logistic model on top ("probability model") so that we can get `.pred_Yes`. SVMs do not produce probabilities natively; this *Platt scaling* is a bolt-on, and its calibration is so-so (Tutorial 6 will show you how to check). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(svm_rbf_fit, dm_train) |> cls_metrics(truth = undx_dm, estimate = .pred_class, .pred_Yes) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: That is the **training** performance — reported only to make a point in *Your turn*. The honest number is below. ## 4 · Honest comparison on the five folds ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) svm_res <- workflow_set( preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = list(linear = svm_lin_spec, poly2 = svm_poly_spec, rbf = svm_rbf_spec) ) |> workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = cls_metrics, seed = 2026, verbose = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` maximum number of iterations reached 0.002334747 -0.002211177 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` maximum number of iterations reached 0.00694341 -0.006086287 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` maximum number of iterations reached 0.0002650637 -0.0002616375 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` line search fails -0.1885002 -1.510117 2.20099e-05 3.454223e-06 -4.066054e-09 -3.471025e-09 -1.014831e-13 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` line search fails -0.1895854 -1.503686 1.876434e-05 2.958768e-06 -3.454534e-09 -2.960713e-09 -7.358211e-14 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} rank_results(svm_res, rank_metric = "roc_auc", select_best = TRUE) |> filter(.metric %in% c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) |> select(wflow_id, .metric, mean, std_err) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} autoplot(svm_res, metric = c("roc_auc", "brier_class")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](03_svm_files/figure-html/cv-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: Three things to notice while it runs: - **It is slower than the forest.** SVM training cost grows roughly with *n²* (every pair of points enters the kernel matrix). 4,000 rows is fine; 400,000 is not. The probability model roughly doubles the time again. - The kernels are usually **within one standard error** of each other here — and of this morning's logistic regression. The simulated truth is close to additive with a few interactions, and a linear SVM on 45 scaled dummies is, in effect, a regularised logistic regression. - Nothing in the output tells you *why* a person was classified. No coefficients you can read (except for the linear kernel), no trees, no importances without the model-agnostic tools of Tutorial 6. ## 5 · Where SVMs fit today SVMs were the best general-purpose classifier from roughly 1995 to 2010. Gradient boosting took that title for tabular data (tomorrow morning) and deep learning took it for images and text. They remain excellent for **small, high-dimensional, clean** problems — gene-expression panels, text classification, some signal problems — and the margin idea underpins a lot of later theory. For survey-type health data you will rarely choose one over XGBoost, but you should be able to fit, tune and explain one when a reviewer asks. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE) saveRDS(svm_res, "outputs/t03_svm_res.rds") # kept for reference; nothing later depends on it ``` ::: ## Your turn (15 min) ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task A · Cost and overfitting Fit `svm_rbf(cost = ___, rbf_sigma = 0.005)` for `cost` in {0.1, 1, 10, 100} with `fit_resamples()` on `dm_folds` (use a `workflow_set()` so it is one call). For each, also record the **training-set** AUC from a plain `fit()` on `dm_train`. Plot or tabulate training AUC and CV AUC against cost. **A1.** Which direction does the gap between training and CV AUC move as cost rises? Why? **A2.** Which cost would you pick, and would you want to try values outside this range? ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution A ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} costs <- c(0.1, 1, 10, 100) svm_costs <- lapply(costs, \(cst) svm_rbf(cost = cst, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |> set_engine("kernlab") |> set_mode("classification")) names(svm_costs) <- paste0("cost_", costs) set.seed(2026) cost_cv <- workflow_set(preproc = list(base = dm_rec), models = svm_costs) |> workflow_map("fit_resamples", resamples = dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc), seed = 2026) cv_auc <- collect_metrics(cost_cv) |> transmute(cost = readr::parse_number(wflow_id), cv_auc = mean, se = std_err) train_auc <- tibble( cost = costs, train_auc = sapply(svm_costs, \(spec) workflow(dm_rec, spec) |> fit(dm_train) |> augment(dm_train) |> roc_auc(undx_dm, .pred_Yes) |> pull(.estimate)) ) left_join(cv_auc, train_auc, by = "cost") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: A1: training AUC climbs toward 1 as cost rises (the margin narrows and the boundary bends around individual points) while CV AUC flattens or falls — the classic overfitting gap. A2: the CV optimum is usually at cost ≈ 1 or below; it is worth probing 0.01–0.3 as well. This is exactly what `tune_grid()` automates tomorrow, on a log scale. ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## Task B · What happens without scaling? (5 min) Build `rec_noscale` = `dm_rec` without `step_normalize()` (impute, dummy, zv only). Because kernlab would silently rescale for you, switch that off with `set_engine("kernlab", scaled = FALSE)` so you see what the kernel actually does with raw units. Resample and compare the CV AUC with the scaled version. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Solution B ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rec_noscale <- recipe(undx_dm ~ ., data = dm_train) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_impute_mode(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |> step_zv(all_predictors()) svm_raw_spec <- svm_rbf(cost = 1, rbf_sigma = 0.005) |> set_engine("kernlab", scaled = FALSE) |> # stop kernlab from standardising internally set_mode("classification") set.seed(2026) noscale_res <- fit_resamples(workflow(rec_noscale, svm_raw_spec), dm_folds, metrics = metric_set(roc_auc, brier_class)) collect_metrics(noscale_res) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Noticeably worse: with `hh_income` in ringgit dominating every distance, the kernel "sees" income and little else. Scaling is not a nicety for distance-based methods (SVMs, neural networks); it is part of the model. (Had you left kernlab's default `scaled = TRUE`, the two recipes would have tied — and you would have learned the wrong lesson. Know what your engine does for you.) ::: ## What to remember 1. SVM = widest possible street between the classes, with a `cost`-controlled tolerance for violations. 2. Kernels bend the street; `rbf_sigma`/`degree` set how much. Both knobs need tuning on a log scale. 3. Numeric + scaled inputs are mandatory. Probabilities are a bolt-on; check their calibration. 4. Slow for large *n*; opaque without model-agnostic explanation tools. **Next (Day 2, 09.15):** Tutorial 4 — gradient boosting with XGBoost, and the bake-off of all four.
